08 · Does higher resolution improve winter precipitation extremes?¶

Question for this notebook. Higher-resolution models cost much more to run. Do they represent extreme precipitation better? And do the conclusions drawn from a model, such as how strongly the NAO drives rainfall extremes, depend on its resolution?

Why this pair of runs. Comparing two different models (ICON-ESM-ER and IFS-FESOM2-SR) mixes resolution with everything else that differs between them. Here the comparison is clean: the same atmosphere model (IFS), with the same observed sea-surface temperature, run at about 9 km (tco1279) and about 28 km (tco399). Only the resolution differs.

Data. Daily precipitation over north-west Europe, winters (December–February) 1986–2014, 29 winters:

  • IFS at 9 km: one run.
  • IFS at 28 km: three members (the first three of the five available, to limit the download).
  • References: E-OBS (station-based, land) and ERA5 (reanalysis, about 31 km).

All four are compared on the same 0.25° grid (about 25 km). This matters: the 9 km run has been averaged onto that grid, so detail finer than about 25 km is not visible here. The question is therefore whether running at 9 km improves precipitation at the 25 km scale, which is the scale at which the models are usually evaluated and used.

How chance is judged. The three 28 km members differ only by chance. A 9 km result counts as a resolution effect only if it lies outside the range of the three 28 km members. With three members that is a weak test, so only clear differences are reported as such.

Background: the terms used in this notebook¶

Term What it means here
Resolution The size of the model's grid boxes. 9 km boxes can represent mountains, coastlines and storms in more detail than 28 km boxes.
tco1279, tco399 ECMWF's names for the 9 km and 28 km grids of the IFS model.
Atmosphere-only run The ocean is not simulated; observed sea-surface temperature is prescribed. Both runs see exactly the same ocean.
Member One of several runs of the same experiment that differ only in tiny details of their starting state. Their differences show how large chance is.
Member range The lowest to the highest value across the three 28 km members.
RX1day, R95p The wettest day of the winter; the rain that falls on very wet days (above the local 95th percentile of wet days). As in notebook 05.
Wet day A day with at least 1 mm.
Quantile (percentile) The value below which a given share of wet days falls. The 99th percentile is exceeded on 1 wet day in 100.
Pattern correlation, RMSE How similar the shape of two maps is (−1 to 1), and the typical size of their local differences.

Colours. Purple: IFS 9 km. Green: IFS 28 km (one line or dot per member). Dark grey: ERA5. Light grey: E-OBS. In difference maps, grey means no difference.

1. Setup and data check¶

What this cell does. Loads the project code and names the datasets.

In [1]:
import sys, warnings
sys.path.insert(0, '../src')
warnings.filterwarnings('ignore')

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import xarray as xr
from eerie_uk import climatology as clim, extremes as ex, nao, plotting, regions, relationships as rel, store

pd.set_option('display.width', 220, 'display.float_format', '{:.2f}'.format)
NAME = plotting.SOURCE_LABELS
HI, LO = 'ifs-amip-tco1279.hist', 'ifs-amip-tco399.hist'
REFS = ['e-obs', 'era5']
WINTERS = (1986, 2014)

What this cell does. Loads the daily precipitation of the two IFS runs and keeps the winter days. Each winter (December–February) is labelled by the year of its January; the first and last incomplete winters are dropped by the index functions.

In [2]:
def winter_days(source):
    da = store.load(source, 'day', 'pr', 'nw_europe')
    return da.sel(time=da.time.dt.month.isin([12, 1, 2]))

hi = winter_days(HI)                      # (time, lat, lon)
lo = winter_days(LO)                      # (time, realization, lat, lon)
print('9 km :', dict(hi.sizes), hi.attrs.get('units'))
print('28 km:', dict(lo.sizes), 'members', list(lo.realization.values), lo.attrs.get('units'))

9 km : {'time': 2707, 'lat': 101, 'lon': 133} mm/day
28 km: {'time': 2707, 'realization': 3, 'lat': 101, 'lon': 133} members [np.int64(1), np.int64(2), np.int64(3)] mm/day

What this cell does. Computes the winter indices for the two IFS runs: the winter mean, RX1day, and R95p with a winter threshold from 1985–2014. For the references the same indices were already computed in notebook 05 and are read from its cache. E-OBS is put on the model grid, and a land mask is built: regional numbers use the same land cells (where E-OBS has data) for everyone.

In [3]:
def winter_indices(pr):
    threshold = ex.wet_day_threshold(pr, period='DJF')
    out = xr.Dataset({'rx1day': ex.rx1day(pr, 'DJF'), 'r95p': ex.r95p(pr, threshold, 'DJF'), 'p95': threshold})
    labels = ex.period_labels(pr.time, 'DJF')
    kept = pr.sel(time=(labels > 0).values)
    out['mean'] = kept.groupby(labels.sel(time=kept.time)).mean('time')
    return out.sel(year=slice(*WINTERS))

ind = {HI: winter_indices(hi), LO: winter_indices(lo)}
for r in REFS:
    cached = ex.indices_for(r)
    daily = winter_days(r)
    labels = ex.period_labels(daily.time, 'DJF')
    kept = daily.sel(time=(labels > 0).values)
    ind[r] = xr.Dataset({'rx1day': cached.rx1day_djf.rename(year_djf='year'), 'r95p': cached.r95p_djf.rename(year_djf='year'),
                         'p95': cached.p95_djf, 'mean': kept.groupby(labels.sel(time=kept.time)).mean('time')}).sel(year=slice(*WINTERS))
grid = ind[HI]
ind['e-obs'] = regions.to_grid(ind['e-obs'], grid)
land = regions.land_mask(grid.lat, grid.lon)
common = land & ind['e-obs'].rx1day.isel(year=0).notnull()
pd.DataFrame([{'dataset': NAME.get(k, k), 'winters': ind[k].sizes['year'], 'members': int(ind[k].sizes.get('realization', 1))} for k in (REFS + [HI, LO])])

2. Findings¶

29 winters, 1986–2014, compared on the same 0.25° grid. IFS at 9 km: one run. IFS at 28 km: three members. Same model, same observed sea-surface temperature.

Land average, winter E-OBS ERA5 9 km 28 km (three members) 9 km relative to 28 km
UK and Ireland: wettest winter day 21.9 mm 20.7 mm 23.7 mm 22.4 to 22.9 mm +5%
UK and Ireland: rain on very wet days 48.8 mm 43.2 mm 51.1 mm 46.0 to 48.8 mm +7%
Western Norway: wettest winter day 39.3 mm 36.8 mm 41.1 mm 36.5 to 37.3 mm +12%
Western Norway: rain on very wet days 97.7 mm 96.8 mm 99.2 mm 84.8 to 92.0 mm +11%
Map error against the reference (RMSE, lower is better) 9 km 28 km members
Wettest winter day vs E-OBS 5.6 mm 5.0 to 5.3 mm
Wettest winter day vs ERA5 4.5 mm 3.1 to 3.3 mm
Rain on very wet days vs E-OBS 12.6 mm 11.1 to 12.0 mm
Correlation of winter R95p with the NAO E-OBS ERA5 9 km 28 km members
UK and Ireland 0.51 0.35 0.19 0.04 to 0.33
Western Norway 0.81 0.81 0.71 0.63 to 0.75
North-west France 0.34 0.28 0.04 −0.38 to 0.28

What this means, in plain words

  1. Higher resolution makes winter rain heavier. At 9 km the wettest winter day and the rain on very wet days are 5–12% larger than at 28 km, and in most places the difference lies outside the range of the three 28 km members. The increase is largest over mountains and west-facing coasts (western Norway, western Scotland, the Alps), where finer terrain lifts moist air more sharply.
  2. Heavier is not automatically better. Over western Norway, where 28 km falls short of both references, 9 km comes closer to them. Over UK and Ireland, where 28 km is already about right, 9 km overshoots. Across the whole region the 9 km maps have a slightly larger typical error than any 28 km member against both references, while the pattern is about equally good (pattern correlations 0.81–0.94 for all runs). At the 25 km scale compared here, running at 9 km brings no overall gain for winter rainfall extremes in this model, and a local gain over steep terrain.
  3. The conclusion about drivers does not depend on resolution, but it does depend on chance. The NAO-to-extremes correlation at 9 km lies within, or close to, the range of the three 28 km members in every region. That range is itself wide: from 0.04 to 0.33 over UK and Ireland, and from −0.38 to +0.28 over north-west France, in runs of the same model with the same ocean. With 29 winters, internal variability alone can change the answer to "how strongly does the NAO drive UK rainfall extremes in this model" more than going from 28 km to 9 km does.
  4. The strong link over western Norway is robust to both: 0.63 to 0.75 in every run, close to both references (0.81).

Answer to the question. In this model, going from 28 km to 9 km makes winter rainfall extremes 5–12% heavier, helps over steep terrain such as western Norway, and does not improve the region as a whole at the 25 km scale. The qualitative conclusion about the NAO's influence does not change with resolution; it is far more sensitive to internal variability, which a single run cannot capture. These are exploratory results from one 9 km run and three 28 km members, for winter only.

3. Winter-mean precipitation¶

What this cell does. Maps the average winter precipitation, 1986–2014, for the two references, the 9 km run and the 28 km run (average of its three members).

In [4]:
def avg(key, var):
    field = ind[key][var].mean('year')
    return field.mean('realization') if 'realization' in field.dims else field
plotting.plot_field_panels({NAME.get(k, k): avg(k, 'mean') for k in REFS + [HI, LO]}, units='mm/day', columns=2,
                           title='Winter (DJF) mean precipitation, 1986-2014');

Figure 1. Average winter precipitation. The 28 km panel is the mean of three members.

What this cell does. Maps the 9 km run minus the 28 km run, as a percentage. Dots mark cells where the 9 km value lies outside the range of the three 28 km members, that is, where the difference is larger than what chance produces between 28 km runs.

In [5]:
def outside(key_hi, var):
    value = ind[key_hi][var].mean('year')
    members = ind[LO][var].mean('year')
    return (value > members.max('realization')) | (value < members.min('realization'))
panels = {f'{var}: 9 km vs 28 km': 100 * (avg(HI, var) - avg(LO, var)) / avg(LO, var) for var in ('mean', 'rx1day')}
plotting.plot_field_panels(panels, units='% difference', diverging=True, columns=2,
                           stipple={f'{var}: 9 km vs 28 km': outside(HI, var) for var in ('mean', 'rx1day')},
                           title='Winter precipitation and wettest winter day: 9 km relative to 28 km');

Figure 2. Orange: wetter at 9 km than at 28 km; blue: drier. Left: winter-mean precipitation. Right: the wettest winter day. Dots: outside the 28 km member range.

What this cell does. Maps the average wettest winter day for the references and both resolutions.

In [6]:
plotting.plot_field_panels({NAME.get(k, k): avg(k, 'rx1day') for k in REFS + [HI, LO]}, units='mm', columns=2,
                           title='Winter RX1day, mean of 1986-2014');

Figure 3. The wettest winter day. Look at the mountains (western Norway, Scotland, the Alps, northern Iberia): this is where resolution should matter most, because higher resolution resolves steeper terrain that forces air upwards.

5. The distribution of daily rainfall¶

What this cell does. Pools all winter wet days over the land of each region and computes the amount below which 50%, 75%, 90%, 95%, 99% and 99.9% of them fall. The curves show the whole heavy end of the distribution, not just a single index.

In [7]:
probabilities = np.array([0.5, 0.75, 0.9, 0.95, 0.99, 0.999])
def wet_quantiles(pr, region):
    box = regions.subset_box(pr.where(common), region)
    values = box.values.ravel()
    values = values[np.isfinite(values) & (values >= ex.WET_DAY)]
    return np.quantile(values, probabilities)

daily = {r: winter_days(r).sel(time=slice('1985-12-01', '2014-02-28')) for r in REFS}
daily['e-obs'] = regions.to_grid(daily['e-obs'], grid)
daily[HI] = hi.sel(time=slice('1985-12-01', '2014-02-28'))
quantiles = {}
for region in regions.SUBREGIONS:
    quantiles[region] = {r: wet_quantiles(daily[r], region) for r in REFS + [HI]}
    for m in lo.realization.values:
        quantiles[region][f'{LO}#{m}'] = wet_quantiles(lo.sel(realization=m).sel(time=slice('1985-12-01', '2014-02-28')), region)
x = np.arange(probabilities.size)      # evenly spaced, so the rare extremes are not squashed
plotting.plot_line_panels({regions.LABELS[r]: {k: (x, v) for k, v in quantiles[r].items()} for r in regions.SUBREGIONS},
                          ylabel='mm/day', xlabel='percentile of winter wet days',
                          title='How heavy are heavy winter rain days? Land, 1986-2014',
                          xticks=(list(x), ['50', '75', '90', '95', '99', '99.9']));

Figure 4. Each line shows how heavy the wettest x% of winter wet days are. The three green lines are the three 28 km members; their spread is chance. The x axis is not to scale: the last points are the rare extremes.

6. Regional numbers¶

What this cell does. Averages each winter index over the land of each region (same cells for all datasets), then over 1986–2014. For the 28 km run it shows the three members' lowest and highest value. The last column says whether the 9 km value lies outside that range.

In [8]:
LABEL = {'mean': 'winter mean (mm/day)', 'rx1day': 'wettest winter day (mm)', 'r95p': 'rain on very wet days (mm)', 'p95': 'very-wet-day threshold (mm/day)'}
def regional(key, var, region):
    field = ind[key][var]
    if 'year' in field.dims:
        field = field.mean('year')
    return clim.regional_mean(field.where(common), region)
rows = []
for region in regions.SUBREGIONS:
    for var, label in LABEL.items():
        members = regional(LO, var, region)
        h = float(regional(HI, var, region))
        rows.append({'region': regions.LABELS[region], 'quantity': label,
                     'E-OBS': float(regional('e-obs', var, region)), 'ERA5': float(regional('era5', var, region)),
                     '9 km': h, '28 km lowest': float(members.min()), '28 km highest': float(members.max()),
                     '9 km outside 28 km range': bool(h < float(members.min()) or h > float(members.max())),
                     '9 km vs 28 km mean %': 100 * (h - float(members.mean())) / float(members.mean())})
regional_table = pd.DataFrame(rows)
regional_table

7. Which resolution is closer to the references?¶

What this cell does. Scores the maps of the winter mean and of RX1day against each reference over land: RMSE (typical local error, lower is better) and pattern correlation (higher is better). The 9 km run is scored once; each 28 km member separately, so the spread shows how much the score itself varies by chance.

In [9]:
rows = []
for var in ('mean', 'rx1day', 'r95p'):
    for ref in REFS:
        reference = avg(ref, var).where(common)
        candidates = {'9 km': ind[HI][var].mean('year')}
        candidates.update({f'28 km member {int(m)}': ind[LO][var].mean('year').sel(realization=m) for m in ind[LO].realization.values})
        for label, field in candidates.items():
            stats = clim.pattern_stats(field.where(common), reference)
            rows.append({'quantity': LABEL[var], 'reference': NAME[ref], 'run': label,
                         'RMSE': stats['rmse'], 'pattern correlation': stats['pattern correlation'], 'mean bias': stats['bias']})
skill = pd.DataFrame(rows)
skill.pivot_table(index=['quantity', 'reference'], columns='run', values='RMSE')

8. Does the NAO-to-extremes conclusion depend on resolution?¶

Notebook 06 asked whether models reproduce the observed link between the winter NAO and winter rainfall extremes. Here the same question is asked of both resolutions: would a scientist using the 9 km run reach a different conclusion from one using the 28 km run?

What this cell does. Builds the winter NAO index of each run and member from monthly pressure, measured along the ERA5 NAO pattern (as in notebooks 04 and 07), and correlates it with the land average of winter R95p in each region, after removing trends. ERA5 and E-OBS use the ERA5 NAO.

In [11]:
era5_eof = nao.leading_eof(nao.winter_anomalies(store.load('era5', 'mon', 'psl', 'north_atlantic')))
def nao_of(source):
    winters = nao.winter_anomalies(store.load(source, 'mon', 'psl', 'north_atlantic'), (1980, 2023))
    return (nao.project(winters, era5_eof.vector) / era5_eof.amplitude).sel(year=slice(*WINTERS))
era5_nao = (nao.project(nao.winter_anomalies(store.load('era5', 'mon', 'psl', 'north_atlantic')), era5_eof.vector) / era5_eof.amplitude).sel(year=slice(*WINTERS))
nao_hi, nao_lo = nao_of(HI), nao_of(LO)

def r95_series(key, region, member=None):
    field = ind[key]['r95p']
    if member is not None:
        field = field.sel(realization=member)
    return clim.regional_mean(field.where(common), region)

rows = []
for region in regions.SUBREGIONS:
    row = {'region': regions.LABELS[region]}
    for r in REFS:
        row[NAME[r]] = rel.regress_series(r95_series(r, region).values, era5_nao.sel(year=r95_series(r, region).year).values)['r']
    row['9 km'] = rel.regress_series(r95_series(HI, region).values, nao_hi.sel(year=r95_series(HI, region).year).values)['r']
    for m in ind[LO].realization.values:
        series = r95_series(LO, region, m)
        row[f'28 km member {int(m)}'] = rel.regress_series(series.values, nao_lo.sel(realization=m, year=series.year).values)['r']
    rows.append(row)
print('29 winters, detrended; a correlation above about 0.38 is significant at the 5% level')
link = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index('region')
link

29 winters, detrended; a correlation above about 0.38 is significant at the 5% level

How to read this table. If the 9 km value sits within the spread of the three 28 km members, the conclusion about the NAO link does not depend on resolution in this model.

9. Limitations¶

  • Three 28 km members, one 9 km run. Only differences that clearly exceed the member range can be attributed to resolution. Smaller real effects would be missed.
  • Winter only. The 28 km download was limited to winter to save network traffic.
  • Compared at 0.25°. Both runs were regridded to about 25 km by the data provider, so any benefit of 9 km below that scale (for example in narrow valleys or convective cells) is not visible.
  • One model, one pair of resolutions. The result is for IFS with prescribed SST, not for coupled models or for other modelling systems.
  • Complexity is not tested. Only resolution changes between these runs.
  • References disagree somewhat (notebook 05): E-OBS smooths station data, ERA5 is itself a model product at about 31 km.

10. Open questions¶

  1. Does the benefit of 9 km over mountains grow when compared at its native resolution, against a high-resolution station dataset?
  2. How many members are needed before the NAO-to-extremes correlation of one configuration can be distinguished from another's?
  3. Do coupled models at different ocean and atmosphere resolutions show the same pattern?
